key_terms.meaning: A pair of thyristors (or a TRIAC) in series with the load on an AC supply; the load voltage is varied by controlling when the device is allowed to conduct in each half cycle.
Delay, measured from the start of each half cycle, before the thyristor is turned on; 0 ≤ α ≤ π radians (0° to 180°).
For a resistive load the device conducts from α to π, so the conduction angle is π − α; with an RL load it extends to the extinction angle β.
V<sub>rms</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>√[(π − α)/π + sin(2α)/(2π)] for a resistive load; V<sub>s</sub> is the supply rms voltage.
The thyristor pair is kept on for n whole supply cycles and off for the remaining N − n cycles; the duty ratio is k = n/N.
V<sub>rms</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>√k, where k = n/N is the fraction of supply cycles in which the load is connected.
A three-terminal bidirectional thyristor that conducts in both half cycles, so the two anti-parallel SCRs are replaced by one device.
The two main terminals of a TRIAC: MT1 is the reference terminal (the one tied to the trigger circuit), MT2 is the other main terminal.
The four combinations of MT2 polarity (positive or negative) and gate pulse polarity; quadrants I and III, where the gate pulse has the same polarity as MT2, are the most sensitive.
A TRIAC fired with the wrong gate pulse polarity in one half cycle; it then gives different delays in the two half cycles, so the output contains a DC component and a larger even harmonic content.
Three single-phase controllers on the three lines, in a star or delta configuration, to control a three-phase load.
A component equal in all three phases that can flow only if a neutral wire exists; with a three-wire star or a delta it cannot flow, so the phase currents are forced to sum to zero.
With no neutral and a balanced resistive load, α can be varied from 0° to 150°; at 150° the output becomes zero.
A switch that rapidly connects the load to the supply and then short-circuits the load, many times per supply cycle, to set the RMS load voltage.
D = t<sub>on</sub>/T<sub>s</sub>, the fraction of one switching period for which the load is connected to the supply; V<sub>rms</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>√D.
The chopper frequency, chosen far above 50 Hz (a few kHz); it fixes where the unwanted sidebands sit, and therefore the size of the filter.
A converter that synthesises a low-frequency AC output by switching the load between two phase-controlled converter groups, one for each output half cycle.
Both converter groups are gated continuously; a current circulates between them and is limited by an intergroup reactor.
Only the group that is due to supply the load is gated; the other is blocked, so no intergroup reactor current flows but the changeover needs a current-zero.
The ratio of output frequency to input frequency f<sub>o</sub>/f<sub>i</sub>; it is usually less than 1 (step-down), and stepped-up operation is possible only over a small range.
Nine bidirectional switches that connect any input phase to any output phase directly, giving amplitude and frequency control with no DC link.
Two IGBTs (or other devices) connected back to back with common emitter or common collector so that current can flow both ways when the switch is on.
For each output phase the three switch duty cycles must sum to one, and the output voltage must stay inside the input voltage envelope.
In linear modulation the output voltage cannot exceed √3/2 ≈ 0.866 times the input voltage.

takeaways: An AC voltage controller changes only the RMS value of a fixed-frequency supply; it never changes the frequency.
Phase control is simple and cheap, but it chops the sine wave, so the load sees harmonics and the supply sees a poor power factor at large α.
On-off control passes or blocks whole cycles, so the load current is always a clean sine when it flows, but the supply current has a low-frequency flicker content.
A TRIAC replaces two SCRs, but the gate pulse polarity must match the MT2 polarity or the two half cycles fire unequally.
A three-phase controller without a neutral cannot carry zero-sequence current, so its control range and waveforms differ from three independent single-phase controllers.
A PWM AC chopper pushes the switching harmonics to kilohertz frequencies, where a small filter removes them, at the cost of more switching loss and an extra switch.
A cycloconverter is a naturally commutated direct frequency changer, mostly used to step the frequency down for large, slow machines.
A matrix converter is an all-silicon direct frequency changer with no DC link, but it needs bidirectional switches and its voltage gain is limited to about 0.866.
bank_note: Long answers here almost always demand a waveform sketch plus a derivation of the RMS output, and a comparison of phase control, on-off control, PWM chopping, cycloconversion and matrix conversion on power factor, harmonics and device count.

bank.q: Explain the working of a single-phase AC voltage controller feeding a resistive load. Define the firing angle and the conduction angle, sketch the supply voltage, gate pulses and load voltage for α = 60°, and derive the expression for the RMS output voltage.
outline: Circuit: anti-parallel SCR pair (or TRIAC) in series with the load across the AC supply
T1 conducts from α to π, T2 from π + α to 2π, so positive and negative half cycles are chopped symmetrically
Definition of α and of conduction angle π − α for a resistive load
Three sketches: supply, gate pulses, output voltage with the shaded chopped region
Derivation: V_rms² = (1/π)∫ V_m² sin²θ dθ from α to π, giving V_rms = V_s√[(π − α)/π + sin(2α)/(2π)]
Limits: α = 0 gives V_rms = V_s, α = π gives zero, and the control is continuous

bank.q: Describe integral-cycle (on-off) control of an AC load. Define the duty ratio k, give the RMS output formula, and state two advantages and two disadvantages compared with phase control.
outline: The thyristor pair is turned on at a zero crossing and kept on for n whole cycles out of every N
Duty ratio k = n/N, and the RMS output is V_s√k
Advantages: no chopped waveform, so the current during conduction is a pure sine with low harmonic content and near-unity displacement factor
Disadvantages: any value of k other than 0 or 1 injects sub-harmonic (low-frequency flicker) components; large N gives slow response
Application: heaters and ovens where thermal inertia smooths the flicker; not for lamps or fast servos

bank.q: With a neat sketch of device structure and characteristics, explain the TRIAC and the four triggering quadrants. Why should the gate pulse polarity suit the MT2 polarity?
outline: Structure: two SCRs in anti-parallel on one chip, terminals MT1, MT2 and gate, MT1 as reference
V-I characteristic: conduction in both directions, with latching and holding current in each direction
Four quadrants defined by MT2 polarity and gate current polarity
Quadrants I and III (gate pulse of the same polarity as MT2) are the most sensitive; quadrant IV is the least sensitive
A pulse of the wrong polarity fires late or not at all, so the two half cycles differ: DC component, even harmonics, possible transformer saturation
Practical rule: use quadrant I/III triggering or a negative gate current train for all quadrants

bank.q: Describe the different configurations of three-phase AC voltage controllers. Why does a three-wire star or delta load behave differently from three independent single-phase controllers?
outline: Configurations: three controllers in each line, star-connected load with neutral, star without neutral, and delta-connected load
Neutral-connected star: each phase is independent, and α has the full 0° to 180° range
Three-wire star or delta: no path for zero-sequence current, so the phase currents must sum to zero and the neutral point of the load shifts
Two devices conduct at a time, and the control range with a resistive load becomes 0° to 150°
Consequences: non-sinusoidal phase voltages, triplen harmonics in the line-to-neutral voltages but not in the line currents
Delta connection: triplen harmonic currents circulate inside the delta and do not reach the supply

bank.q: A 230 V, 50 Hz supply feeds a 20 Ω resistor through an anti-parallel SCR pair. For α = 90°, calculate the RMS output voltage, the RMS current and the power delivered. Also state the power factor.
outline: Use V_rms = V_s√[(π − α)/π + sin(2α)/(2π)] with α = π/2
Power factor = V_rms/V_s = 0.707 (resistive load, displacement factor unity but distortion present)

bank.q: A 230 V, 50 Hz heater of 20 Ω is fed through a pair of thyristors using integral-cycle control, 25 on-cycles out of every 100. Find the RMS voltage, the power and the input power factor. State the fundamental frequency of the supply current envelope.
outline: Duty ratio k = n/N = 25/100 = 0.25
Power factor ≈ √k = 0.5
On-off pattern repeats every N = 100 cycles = 2 s, giving envelope components at 0.5 Hz and its multiples, not at 50 Hz

bank.q: A PWM AC chopper feeds a resistive load from a 230 V, 50 Hz supply. Find the duty ratio needed for an output of 184 V RMS, and explain how the switching frequency is chosen with respect to the filter.
outline: The chopper connects the load to the supply for D·T_s and short-circuits the load for (1 − D)T_s
Switching sidebands appear around f_sw ± 2f_supply and their multiples, well above 50 Hz
A small low-pass LC filter at the load removes them; filter size falls as f_sw rises
Trade-off: higher f_sw reduces filter size but increases switching loss and EMI
The freewheel switch must be bidirectional (two devices back to back) to carry the load current in both half cycles

bank.q: A single-phase step-down cycloconverter using two bridge converter groups is to produce 12.5 Hz from a 50 Hz supply feeding an RL load. Explain the firing-angle pattern of each group and sketch the output voltage.
outline: Frequency ratio f_o/f_i = 12.5/50 = 1/4, so one output cycle spans four supply cycles
Positive group is phase-controlled with α varying slowly to trace the positive half sine; the negative group traces the negative half
Firing angle is modulated as α(t) chosen so that the average output follows V_o sin(2πf_o t)
Group changeover at the output current zero, or continuous gating with an intergroup reactor
Output waveform is a series of supply-frequency segments whose average is the low-frequency sine; the ripple is at f_i and its harmonics plus f_o sidebands
For an RL load the current is nearly sinusoidal at f_o because the load inductance filters the segments

bank.q: A three-phase to three-phase matrix converter uses nine bidirectional switches. Explain the switching constraints, state the maximum voltage gain, and find the highest output line voltage available from a 400 V line supply.
outline: Nine switches, each made of two IGBTs back to back (18 devices), one for every input-phase/output-phase pair
Constraint 1: never short two input lines, so at most one switch per output phase is on
Constraint 2: the load must never be open-circuited (inductive load), so exactly one switch per output phase is on at all times
Duty cycles for the three switches feeding one output phase sum to one
Linear modulation limit gives a voltage transfer ratio of √3/2 ≈ 0.866
Highest output line voltage ≈ 0.866 × 400 ≈ 346 V

bank.q: A 400 V, 50 Hz three-phase supply feeds a star-connected resistive load of 40 Ω per phase through three anti-parallel SCR pairs, with the neutral connected. For α = 120°, find the per-phase RMS voltage, the per-phase power and the total power. State what changes if the neutral is removed.
outline: With neutral, each phase is an independent single-phase controller
Per-phase power = 102²/40 ≈ 260 W, total ≈ 780 W
Without neutral, zero-sequence current cannot flow, the neutral point of the load shifts, the control range becomes 0° to 150°, and the phase voltages are no longer equal at large α

bank.q: Compare phase control, integral-cycle control and PWM AC chopping for a 1 kW lamp dimmer on a 230 V supply, on harmonic content, power factor, flicker, acoustic noise and filter requirement. Recommend one for a domestic dimmer and justify.
outline: Phase control: continuous, cheapest, but high harmonic distortion and power factor falling with α; produces buzz in lamps and radio interference
Integral-cycle: clean current during conduction, unity displacement factor, but visible flicker unless the repetition rate is high; unsuitable for lighting
PWM chopper: output harmonics pushed to kilohertz; small filter needed; extra switch, switching loss and EMI
Comparison table of THD, PF, response speed, device count, filter size
For a domestic dimmer, phase control with a TRIAC wins on cost, size and continuity; PWM is used where low harmonic injection is mandated
Mention the practical add-on: an LC or EMI choke and snubber

bank.q: Distinguish circulating-current and non-circulating-current modes of a dual converter used as a cycloconverter. Discuss the effect of each on output waveform quality, intergroup reactor size and changeover time.
outline: Circulating mode: both groups gated continuously, firing angles set so their mean voltages are equal and opposite, current limited by an intergroup reactor
Advantages: changeover is instantaneous, no dead time, better low-frequency output, the load current is continuous
Disadvantages: reactor must carry the circulating current, poorer efficiency, larger equipment
Non-circulating mode: the idle group is blocked and fired only after the load current reaches zero and a small dead time passes
Advantages: no reactor, better efficiency
Disadvantages: dead time distorts the output at low output frequency, slower response, needs reliable current-zero detection
Conclusion: circulating mode suits low output frequencies; non-circulating suits moderate frequencies and higher efficiency

bank.q: A 5 Hz to 20 Hz, three-phase induction motor drive is to be fed from a 50 Hz, 400 V supply. Evaluate three options: a cycloconverter, a matrix converter, and a rectifier plus PWM inverter. Choose one and justify with device count, efficiency and control range.
outline: Cycloconverter: naturally commutated, rugged, handles large power, no DC link; but many thyristors, poor input power factor at low output voltage, output frequency limited to about f_i/3
Matrix converter: no DC link, bidirectional power flow, sinusoidal input current, 18 IGBTs for a 3×3 array, gain limited to 0.866 and complex commutation
Rectifier–inverter: mature, wide frequency range, cheap, but has a DC-link capacitor (bulk, finite life) and only unidirectional power flow unless made active-front-end
For 5 to 20 Hz the cycloconverter's f_o ≤ f_i/3 limit is met, so it is technically feasible; for a small drive the rectifier–inverter is cheaper and smaller

Recommendation by size: cycloconverter for multi-megawatt slow mills and cement kilns; rectifier–inverter for general industrial drives; matrix converter where regeneration and DC-link-free design are needed
A scoring table on cost, efficiency, input current quality and reliability

bank.q: Derive the input power factor of a single-phase phase-controlled AC controller with a resistive load as a function of α. Discuss how the harmonic content of the supply current affects the supply transformer and the neutral conductor in a three-phase installation.
outline: PF = V_rms/V_s = √[(π − α)/π + sin(2α)/(2π)] for a resistive load
Displacement factor is unity; the whole reduction comes from distortion, so PF = 1/√(1 + THD²)
Current waveform is a chopped sine; Fourier analysis gives odd harmonics only, of significant amplitude
Effect on transformer: extra eddy-current and stray losses, derating, possible overheating of the neutral in three-phase four-wire systems carrying triplen harmonics
Triplen harmonics add in the neutral instead of cancelling, so the neutral current can exceed the phase current
Remedies: passive filter tuned near the 3rd and 5th harmonic, PWM chopper operation, or line-side active filter

glossary.def: A circuit that varies the RMS voltage applied to a load from a fixed-frequency AC supply, without changing the frequency.
Delaying the turn-on of the thyristor within each half cycle so that only a part of the sine wave reaches the load.
The electrical angle, measured from the start of the half cycle, at which the thyristor is triggered.
The angle at which the load current falls to zero and the device turns off; for a resistive load β = π.
The angular interval during which the device conducts, equal to β − α.
On-off control in which the load is connected for whole supply cycles and disconnected for whole supply cycles.
In on-off control, the ratio n/N of conducting cycles to total cycles; the RMS output becomes V_s√k.
A bidirectional three-terminal thyristor that can conduct current in either direction from a single gate pulse.
The two main terminals of a TRIAC; MT1 is the reference terminal for the gate circuit.
One of four operating conditions of a TRIAC, defined by the polarity of MT2 and of the gate current.
Equal firing delay in both half cycles, so the output contains no DC component and only odd harmonics.
An anti-parallel thyristor pair, or a TRIAC, used to connect and disconnect an AC load without moving contacts.
A current component identical in all three phases that can flow only when a neutral or delta path exists.
Three single-phase controllers arranged in the three lines of a three-phase supply, with the load in star or delta.
A converter that switches the load rapidly between the supply and a short circuit to control the RMS load voltage.
The fraction of one switching period for which the load is connected to the supply in a PWM chopper; V_rms = V_s√D.
The rate at which a chopper switch operates, chosen far above the supply frequency to place harmonics where they are easy to filter.
An LC network at the load that passes the 50 Hz component and blocks the switching-frequency sidebands.
A direct frequency changer that builds a low-frequency output from segments of the input voltage by phase control.
Current that flows between two converter groups of a dual converter when both are gated at once, limited by an intergroup reactor.
An inductor placed between the two converter groups of a circulating-current dual converter to limit the current that flows between them.
An array of nine bidirectional switches giving direct AC-to-AC conversion with independent control of output amplitude and frequency.
Two unidirectional devices connected back to back so that the combination blocks and conducts in both directions.
The ratio of output voltage amplitude to input voltage amplitude; in a matrix converter it is limited to about 0.866 in linear modulation.
